articles.title: The Word Worm: How One Hidden Line Turns Microsoft 365 Copilot Into a Self-Propagating Attack
articles.subtitle: A 144-day disclosure ends with a prompt-injection technique that hijacks Copilot for Word, silently rewrites your documents and copies itself into every file the AI touches — surviving two Microsoft fixes.
articles.summary: On July 28, 2026, Norwegian data scientist Håkon Måløy publicly disclosed a technique that turns Microsoft 365 Copilot for Word into the carrier of a self-propagating "AI worm" [1][2]. The attack needs no malware, no macros and no access to the victim's Microsoft account. A single line of hidden text inside a shared Word document is enough: Copilot reads it, obeys it, manipulates the document being drafted — and then copies the hidden instructions into the resulting file, turning that file into a new carrier.

toc.title: What makes this different from every Word threat before it
How the attack works, stage by stage
The disclosure: 144 days, two failed fixes
Why patching is so hard — and why the timing matters
What users and organizations can do now

articles.bodyHtml:
Summary

On July 28, 2026, Norwegian data scientist Håkon Måløy publicly disclosed a technique that turns Microsoft 365 Copilot for Word into the carrier of a self-propagating "AI worm" [1][2]. The attack needs no malware, no macros and no access to the victim's Microsoft account. A single line of hidden text inside a shared Word document is enough: Copilot reads it, obeys it, manipulates the document being drafted — and then copies the hidden instructions into the resulting file, turning that file into a new carrier.

Måløy reported the issue to Microsoft on March 6, 2026. After a 144-day coordinated disclosure, two Microsoft mitigation attempts — blocking the exact prompt wording and upgrading the underlying model — both failed to close the vulnerability class. As of publication, it remains reproducible, and no CVE or standalone Microsoft advisory exists [3][4][5]. This article reconstructs the attack, the timeline, why it resists patching, and what users and organizations can do today.

Note on naming: this is the third and final part of Måløy's "Context Collapse" research series on cross-domain prompt injection (XPIA) against Microsoft 365 Copilot — earlier parts targeted Copilot Memory and Copilot in Outlook, both of which Microsoft fixed. The Word variant is the one that remains open [6].

What makes this different from every Word threat before it

For 25 years, the Word-document threat model was stable: malicious documents carried code — macros, embedded objects, exploits — and defenses focused on blocking execution. User awareness training reduced it to one rule: don't enable macros.

The Word Worm carries no code at all. Its payload is a natural-language sentence, addressed to the AI assistant, not to the user. The execution environment is not Word — it's Copilot's context window, where untrusted document content and the user's trusted instructions are processed side by side. That confusion between data and instructions is the textbook definition of cross-domain prompt injection (XPIA) [3][7].

Two properties elevate it from "yet another prompt injection" to something qualitatively new [2][7][8]:

  1. Self-propagation. The hidden prompt instructs Copilot to copy the prompt itself into the newly generated or edited document, concealed with the same invisible formatting. Every Copilot-touched document becomes a fresh carrier.
  2. Provenance break. Once the instruction lives inside an ordinary, internally generated file, the attacker's original document is no longer involved. The malicious lineage becomes practically untraceable — the carriers are legitimate files, created by legitimate employees, shared through legitimate channels (SharePoint, Teams, OneDrive, email).

Even Simon Willison — who tracks prompt-injection research closely — noted this is the first case he's seen where hidden instructions "deliberately copy themselves to self-replicate" [9].

How the attack works, stage by stage

Stage 1 — Concealment. The attacker hides instructions in a Word document as white text on a white background, set in a tiny font (8 pt in the proof of concept). Structurally the prompt is JSON-formatted and consists of two parts: one instruction that manipulates content, and one that orders Copilot to re-embed the full prompt — in the PoC disguised as an innocuous "source-tracking rule" [2][3][7].

Stage 2 — The trust-boundary crossing. The victim doesn't need to open the booby-trapped file with any special action. Two paths suffice: the employee attaches the document as reference material for a Copilot drafting or editing task ("Edit with Copilot"), or Copilot retrieves the file on its own while searching the victim's OneDrive for relevant material [3][4][10]. In the PoC, the victim merely asked Copilot to write a Q1 financial report for a fictional company; Copilot searched OneDrive by itself and pulled in the poisoned file [4].

Stage 3 — Manipulation. Copilot strips formatting before processing document text — so the white-on-white trick that hides the payload from the human eye is fully transparent to the model. The hidden text is treated as part of the user's request. In the demonstration, Copilot silently halved the financial figures in the report being drafted [1][2][4].

Stage 4 — Replication. Following the second instruction, Copilot appends the entire hidden prompt to the new document, again invisibly formatted [2][7].

Stage 5 — Propagation. The compromised report circulates internally as a trusted file. When a colleague later uses it as source material for another Copilot session, the hidden prompt fires again, alters the new content, and embeds itself once more. The chain continues without the original attacker document — and, importantly, without any further attacker involvement [2][3][5].

The honest caveat: this is not a self-executing internet worm. Each hop requires an additional Copilot drafting or editing operation in which a carrier enters the model's context. The propagation speed is bounded by how intensively an organization uses Copilot — which, given current adoption, is little comfort (see §4) [2][5].

The disclosure: 144 days, two failed fixes

The disclosure process itself was unusually long — 144 days instead of the customary 90 — reflecting how difficult the problem is to remediate [5][10]. Microsoft's public position is a defense-in-depth strategy that blocks malicious instructions "at multiple points," including jailbreak and cross-prompt-injection classifiers — though Microsoft itself acknowledges these may not be available in every Copilot scenario [3][11]. Notably, Microsoft made the blunter version of this argument itself in June 2026, writing that "prompting alone is not a reliable security boundary" [2].

Why patching is so hard — and why the timing matters

Måløy's core argument is architectural. For a model to detect a malicious instruction inside document content, it must read that content — and the act of reading already lets the attacker's words shape the model's judgment. His analogy: relying on the model to catch the attack is like "asking an interpreter to execute an untrusted program to determine whether that program is safe to execute." Adding a second supervisory model produces the same problem one layer up — "LLMs all the way down" [2].

That makes this a class of vulnerability rather than a bug with a patch. Wordings can be blocklisted (Mitigation 1) and models swapped (Mitigation 2), but reworded natural-language instructions sail through — as the GPT-5.6 reproduction demonstrated within a day [2][3][5].

The blast radius context is what elevates this from research curiosity to boardroom topic [2]:

  • Microsoft reports more than 30 million paid Copilot seats, with Copilot revenue up 60% quarter-over-quarter and weekly usage rivaling Outlook and Teams.
  • On the same week's earnings call, Satya Nadella confirmed a unified Copilot "super app" — chat, coding and autonomous agents in one product — launching this year.
  • The carriers travel exactly where enterprise trust lives: SharePoint, Teams, OneDrive. No perimeter tool inspects a "clean" internal .docx for hidden natural-language instructions, because until now that category didn't exist.

Nor is this an isolated finding. It caps a run of Copilot security research in 2026: Måløy's own three-part "Context Collapse" series [6], and Varonis' June disclosure of a Copilot data-extraction chain ("parameter-to-prompt injection") in which a crafted link made Copilot search a user's emails for sensitive material [11]. The pattern across all of them is the same: AI assistants that reach into corporate data keep springing the same kind of trust-boundary leak.

What users and organizations can do now

There is no setting that fully eliminates this vulnerability class [5][7][8]. The realistic mitigations:

For individual users:

  • Treat every external document as untrusted by default — especially anything you plan to feed to Copilot as reference material.
  • Reveal hidden text before attaching: Ctrl+A, then set all text color to black (white-on-white payloads become instantly visible). Check the end of documents — that's where the PoC hid its instructions.
  • Review Copilot-drafted and Copilot-edited documents before sending or reusing them. Verify figures against the original source — silent numeric manipulation was the demonstrated payload.
  • If you don't use Copilot in Word, you can turn it off: File → Options → Copilot → clear "Enable Copilot"; cloud-powered AI features can further be reduced via File → Account → Account Privacy → Manage Settings → uncheck "Turn on optional connected experiences" [7].

For organizations and admins:

  • Establish a policy for which documents may be used as Copilot source material; external files should be the exception, not the default [7][11].
  • Monitor and log Copilot document access and modifications — without this, provenance loss makes incident response close to impossible [3].
  • Watch for Microsoft's classifier coverage (jailbreak/XPIA classifiers are not available in every Copilot scenario) and demand clarity on which surfaces are covered [3][11].
  • Red-team your own workflows the way Måløy did: the replication test (does a hidden instruction survive one Copilot-assisted hop?) is reproducible without advanced tooling.
  • Update awareness training: "don't enable macros" is no longer the complete sentence. The 2026 version is "verify what the AI read, and what it wrote."

The takeaway

The Word Worm completes a pattern this newsletter has been tracking: AI systems have become a trusted delivery mechanism for attacks. Phantom squatting abused the AI's confident hallucinations to route users to attacker infrastructure. The Word Worm abuses the AI's obedient reading to rewrite documents and replicate through the most trusted channels in the enterprise. In both cases, the exploit does not target the machine. It targets the trust relationship between you and your assistant.

Until models can reliably separate instructions from data — and Microsoft itself says prompting alone can't do it — the operative rule is:

Trust the document, not the assistant. Verify both.

articles.bodyHtml:
Summary

Large language models don't just hallucinate facts — they hallucinate infrastructure. When asked for a company's support page, login portal or developer endpoint, LLMs routinely invent URLs that look plausible but resolve nowhere. New research from Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 quantifies this at scale: across 685,339 prompts about 913 global brands, two LLM families generated 2.1 million URLs — and 37.28% of them (809,455) pointed to domains that do not exist [1].

Attackers have noticed. By monitoring LLM outputs, registering the hallucinated domains before anyone else does, and deploying phishing kits and malware on them, threat actors let the victim's own trusted AI assistant deliver the attack. Unit 42 calls this vector phantom squatting and documented it being weaponized in the wild — in one case 23 days after the model invented the domain, in another 51 days [1]. This article breaks down the study, the documented cases and what users, developers and organizations can realistically do about it.

What phantom squatting is — and how we got here

Domain abuse has evolved in three stages:

  1. Typosquatting exploited human error — one wrong keystroke and you land on a lookalike domain.
  2. Slopsquatting exploited AI error in code — LLMs hallucinate nonexistent software package names, and attackers register those packages so coding assistants later recommend them [7][8][9].
  3. Phantom squatting exploits AI error in links — LLMs hallucinate nonexistent web domains, and attackers register them so chatbots, AI browsers and autonomous agents send users there directly [1].

The critical difference from classic phishing: there is no phishing email, no malicious ad and no watering hole. The delivery mechanism is a system the victim already trusts and their organization has often formally sanctioned [1].

The study: methodology in brief

Unit 42 built a multi-agent discovery framework designed to simulate exactly what an attacker would do [1]:

  • A Query Agent researched each brand's real products, portals and developer resources, then generated realistic prompts deliberately exploiting known LLM failure modes — premise acceptance, authority-framing compliance and the models' tendency to complete narratives with authoritative-sounding but fictitious details. Near-duplicate prompts were removed with Jaccard-similarity filtering, leaving 685,339 prompts across 913 brands.
  • A URL Creator Agent ran the prompts across two production LLM families — a mini-class enterprise model (released April 2025, "LLM1") and a lite-class frontier model (released June 2025, "LLM2") — at three temperature settings each: precise (T = 0.1), balanced (T = 0.7) and creative (T = 1.5).
  • A Verification Pipeline classified every URL using threat intelligence, live content crawling with deep-learning models, and ownership analysis. High-confidence phantom domains were placed on a watchlist to monitor real-world registrations.

Two findings from the design are worth underlining. First, both models shipped before the malicious domains later observed in the wild were registered — proof that the phantom domains were produced by the models' internal language patterns, not memorized from training data [1]. Second, the researchers ranked hallucinated domains by "thermal hallucination persistence" (does the domain appear even at T = 0.1?) and "cross-model consensus" (do different architectures invent the same domain?). Both properties make the attack surface measurable — and therefore predictable for attackers and defenders alike [1].

The findings, by the numbers

The anatomy of the hallucinations matters, too. Of the 809,455 nonexistent URLs, 49.7% were path-level inventions (a plausible path on a real, registered domain), 39.5% were subdomain-level, and 10.8% were pure domain-level hallucinations — entirely unregistered root domains that anyone can buy for a few dollars [1]. The two model families behaved differently: LLM1 skewed toward path-level inventions (56.6%), while LLM2 produced far more subdomain- (45.1%) and domain-level hallucinations (20.0%) — meaning the registerable attack surface depends heavily on which AI a victim uses. Higher temperature settings produced more invented domains, not fewer [12].

The attack lifecycle

Unit 42 describes a three-phase lifecycle [1]:

Register — speed beats reputation. Once attackers harvest high-consensus hallucinated domains (they can probe the same public models the researchers did), registration is cheap and instant. In observed telemetry, domains went from registration to actively serving malicious content within hours. In the Montana Empire case, the phishing kit was staged server-side before the domain was even registered.

Lure — the AI becomes the delivery mechanism. After registration, nothing more is required from the attacker. Any user — or autonomous AI agent — whose query triggers the hallucinated URL receives "an authoritative, high-confidence recommendation to navigate directly to attacker-controlled infrastructure" [1]. Users are measurably more willing to trust a link provided by their AI assistant than one arriving via unsolicited email or text [3][6].

Bypass — the zero-reputation problem. Anti-phishing defenses largely run on domain reputation: blocklists, threat feeds, historical scores. A brand-new domain has none of that. It is "indistinguishable from any legitimate new domain" until enough victims generate telemetry — by which time the damage is done. Realistic SSL certificates come free, and sophisticated operators extend the blind window with redirect cloaking (benign content for crawlers, payloads for humans) and CAPTCHA-gating [1][2].

Documented real-world cases

Unit 42 defines the Adversarial Exploitation Window (AEW) as the time between the first hallucination event and the attacker's registration. Positive AEW = defenders got there first. Both flagship cases below registered positive.

Case 1 — "Montana Empire" phishing kit (AEW: 23 days). On March 8, 2026, the research pipeline generated 13 hallucinated URLs for a lookalike of a national postal service's e-commerce marketplace — across both LLM families and all temperature settings, including the near-deterministic T = 0.1. The domain was watchlisted. On March 31, an adversary registered it and deployed a working phishing kit impersonating the marketplace; the pipeline detected the registration the same day [1].

Forensics showed the kit itself was built with an AI coding assistant (its project directory shipped inside the kit archive). The attacker used it to scrape legitimate storefronts, engineer a PHP backend and build a Telegram-based command-and-control channel for real-time credential exfiltration. The kit features dual-channel interception of credit cards and bank transfers (IBANs rotated via Telegram bot commands), harvesting of national ID data, and an operator console — branded "MONTANA" with the motto Kimseye Güvenme ("Trust No One") — for manually relaying one-time passwords [1][10].

Case 2 — Postal-service Android malware (AEW: 51 days). On February 18, 2026, the pipeline flagged hallucinated URLs for admin.[redacted]post-app[.]com, again across five model/configuration tiers including T = 0.1. On April 10 — 51 days later — an attacker registered the domain and launched a pixel-accurate clone of the national postal service's site, complete with the brand's exact HTML hex colors and fabricated social proof (4.8 stars, "2M+ users") to push downloads of a malicious Android APK [1][10].

Four additional redacted detections (a -login.com, a benefitsportal.com, an -es.org, a business.com and an empresas.com pattern) confirm the vector is being exploited across brands and languages, not as a one-off [1].

Why this can't simply be patched away

Three structural properties make phantom squatting durable:

  1. Hallucination is a side effect of how LLMs generate text, not a bug in any single product. Unit 42 calls it "a structural property of LLM architectures that remains inherently unpatchable" [1][11]. Better grounding and retrieval can reduce it; they cannot eliminate it.
  2. Convergence makes it predictable. When independent model architectures invent the same domain for the same brand — even at near-zero temperature — that domain is effectively pre-destined. Attackers don't need insider access; they can map the hallucination surface with the same public APIs everyone else uses [1].
  3. The supply chain is automating the victim side. AI coding assistants already invent dependencies and endpoints inside the SDLC; agentic workflows fetch URLs with no human in the loop. A hallucinated domain followed autonomously can leak API keys or execute attacker instructions without anyone ever "clicking" [1][11].

What actually helps

For users:

  • Treat every AI-generated link as unverified by default. Type known domains yourself; find services via the official app or an independent search — never via the chat window.
  • The confidence of the answer says nothing about the existence of the URL. Subdomain hallucinations (support.realbrand-help.com) look especially legitimate [1].

For developers and security teams:

  • Don't let agents or copilots auto-follow model-generated URLs. Enforce domain allowlists or human approval for outbound fetches, package installs and webhook endpoints [1].
  • Log and alert on LLM-suggested domains that fail DNS resolution — a spike of "invented" domains related to your brand is an early-warning signal.

For brands and organizations (the Unit 42 recommendation):

  • Proactively map what LLMs hallucinate for your brand (the methodology above is reproducible with public APIs), pre-register the highest-consensus phantom domains, and redirect them to your real properties [1][4].
  • Monitor new-domain registration feeds against your hallucination map. In both documented cases, same-day detection of the registration event was achieved — that's the window where takedowns still work [1].
  • Feed confirmed phantom domains to the security community; Unit 42 shared its findings through the Cyber Threat Alliance, and DNS-security/URL-filtering vendors have begun adding detections [1].

The strategic picture Unit 42 leaves us with is a race: the hallucination surface is predictable for both sides. Whoever maps and registers first — defender or adversary — wins each individual domain [1][11].

The takeaway

Phantom squatting inverts the trust model of the web. We spent two decades teaching people not to trust links from strangers. Now the dangerous link comes from the most trusted software in the building — your AI assistant — delivered with total confidence. Until models stop inventing infrastructure, the rule is simple:

Verify the domain, not the confidence.
